description: We are two developers from Brazil building a game where players design, launch and manage a space mission, balancing mass, power, budget, data and time. Silvio is a software developer and SaaS builder; Carlos is a Business Information Systems graduate focused on systems analysis and rules. We're looking for a UI/UX designer, a game/animation developer and someone with a space science background. Beginners welcome!
summary:
Tupi Orbit is a free browser game where players found a space agency and design complete space missions, from Earth orbit to the Moon and Mars. Each mission has five steps: choose the science objective, build the spacecraft and its instruments, choose the orbit and the rocket, fly the simulation, and read the final report.

Every choice changes six resources at the same time: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. A better camera returns more science, but it also makes the spacecraft heavier, uses more power, produces more data and costs more. When a mission fails, the game explains why in plain words, with the numbers ("Your spacecraft is 10 kg too heavy") and a hint to fix it.

This matters because students rarely get to try a whole mission: they learn orbits, rockets and instruments separately and never see how one decision affects another. Tupi Orbit makes these trade-offs playable and shows there is no single right answer. A Mission Library with real NASA facts and images connects the game to real missions. The game is available in English, Portuguese and Spanish.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

- Campaign: the player picks a country (the 2026 Space Apps partner countries, plus Europe and the United States) and an agency focus, then unlocks three phases in order: Observe Earth (easy), Explore the Moon (medium) and Study Mars (hard). Each phase has a science question, a budget, a deadline and a science goal.

- In each phase the player builds a spacecraft with instruments, a solar panel and an antenna, chooses the orbit and the rocket, and launches. The launch is paid from the agency's funds, even when it fails.

- Free mission: any of the three missions without an agency, for classes and demos.

- Team play: 1 to 4 players, each with a role (Mission Director, Science Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Communications), on one device or each on their own device with a room code. The whole team votes GO / NO-GO before launch.

- Mission Library: 7 real missions and 7 topics (orbits, communications, power, space weather, CubeSats and more), with real NASA images and a link to the official source of every fact.

- Badges: 16 mission patches that reward good engineering and learning habits, such as succeeding after a failure.

HOW IT WORKS

- A rules engine recalculates the six resources after every choice. It checks that the spacecraft fits the rocket for that orbit and that power, budget, data and time all close.

- Before launch, a GO / NO-GO checklist shows what is still wrong, with the numbers. The player can launch anyway, because failing also teaches.

- During the flight, random events (solar storm, launch delay, ground station outage, Mars dust storm) only hurt designs that left too little margin. This teaches why engineers keep margins. The same design always meets the same events, so players can compare changes fairly.

- A 3D view shows the spacecraft changing with every part, then the launch, the trip and the orbit. Without WebGL, the game shows a 2D version and stays playable.

- The report gives a score from 0 to 100, explains what worked and what failed, and shows real NASA missions similar to the player's design, such as Landsat 9, LRO, LCROSS, MRO, 2001 Mars Odyssey and MAVEN.

- A "Learn" box in each step and a quiz at the end reinforce one concept at a time.

- Between missions, side jobs bring funds or science, research improves parts, and agency events help or hurt.

BENEFITS

- Free, runs in the browser, no install and no login, on a laptop or a phone.

- Made for teenagers and young adults (about 14 to 29 years old) and for teachers. All texts use plain language.

- Three languages: English, Portuguese and Spanish. Translations change only the words, never the rules or the numbers, and an automated test guarantees this.

- SI units, as NASA uses in its own projects.

INTENDED IMPACT

A 20 to 40 minute class activity where students discuss real engineering trade-offs ("Why did you choose that rocket?") and learn that a failed mission is a step toward a better design.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Failure is part of the game: every failed mission becomes an explanation and a reason to redesign.

- There is no single right answer. Automated tests check that every mission keeps several winning designs.

- The team roles and the GO / NO-GO vote turn a classroom into a small mission control.

- Simplified game values and real NASA facts are kept apart, so players always know what is real.

WHAT THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Accessibility: weak school laptops and phones, no account, playable with sound off, and a 2D fallback.

- Honesty: game numbers are inspired by real instruments and rockets but simplified, and the game says so. Real facts come only from official pages and each one links to its source.

- Learning design based on Kolb, Knowles, Vygotsky, Papert, Gee, Kapur, Freire, and Black & Wiliam.

- NASA media guidelines: NASA is credited, and no NASA logo or insignia is used.

TOOLS

- Plain JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, built with Vite.

- Vitest for automated tests of the rules, the data and the translations.

- Three.js for the 3D view, loaded only when needed so the game opens fast.

- PeerJS (WebRTC) for team play on several devices.

- flag-icons for country flags; B612 and Big Shoulders Stencil fonts (Google Fonts); Web Audio API for sounds synthesized in the browser (no audio files).

- GitHub Pages for hosting; the code is open on GitHub.

- Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as an AI assistant during development.

- Google Gemini for Commander Capi's AI-generated images and voice (text-to-speech in Google AI Studio, voice Sulafat).
